transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-18
Start time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Vertex - ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Vertex - Platform), Nora Kim (Vertex - Product)

Summary:
Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on quantization profiles (INT8 vs FP8), quality vs latency tradeoffs, and planning a short pilot to benchmark Vertex's NLU model. Customer cares about latency SLOs for real-time chat (<= 120 ms tail), cost targets, and data residency/SOC2.

Topics:
- Overview of Redwood Optimize quantization profiles
- INT8 vs FP8 quality regressions and latency improvements
- Batching, KV cache impacts on tail latency
- Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs for throughput and isolation
- Pilot plan and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): hi everyone, thanks for taking the time, um this is Sofia from Redwood, with Marco our SE. how's everybody doing?
[00:12] Priya (Vertex): good, thanks. excited to get into the quant stuff, we have been looking at int8 and fp8 for a while.
[00:20] Marco (Redwood SE): awesome. quick agenda real quick: overview of quant profiles, show recent benchmarks, then we'll walk through how that maps to latency and quality numbers, and finish with pilot steps. sound good?
[00:32] Liam (Vertex): yep. just to set context, our main requirement is sub 120ms p95 for chat completions, and cost per request target around $0.003. We're flexible on model size but can't accept large quality regressions.
[00:48] Marco: noted. and your stack today? are you running on prem or cloud?
[00:52] Priya: we're hybrid; model training in house, but serving currently on GCP with k8s. privacy team prefers VPC options for production.
[01:05] Sofia: perfect that's a common pattern. Redwood Dedicated or Private map well there; we'll talk about options. quick note: some transcription audio might be off, I might say "K-V cash" sometimes, sorry for the auto trans.
[01:18] Marco: ok jumping into slides — our quantization profiles are what we call baseline int8, aggressive int8, and fp8 hybrid. baseline int8 is safe across most LLMs; aggressive int8 pushes ranges and can introduce minor score drift. fp8 hybrid keeps higher precision for sensitive layers, which often gives the best quality/latency sweet spot.
[01:41] Priya: when you say "minor score drift" how do you quantify that? like rouge/accuracy or embedding cosine?
[01:48] Marco: good question — depends on task. for generation NLG we look at human evals and automated metrics like ROUGE or BLEU where applicable, but for your NLU intent classification we'd run labeled accuracy and embedding cosine similarity tests. typically baseline int8 shows <1% accuracy delta, aggressive int8 can be 1-3% depending on architecture, while fp8 hybrid tends to be <0.5% delta but with slightly higher latency than int8.
[02:11] Nora (Vertex): so fp8 has higher latency than int8? I thought the idea was fp8 reduces compute?
[02:16] Marco: yes it's nuanced — fp8 reduces memory and can speed throughput, but on some hardware fp8 kernels aren't as optimized as int8 yet. also sequence length and KV cache behavior impact observed latency strongly. often int8 gives best single-request latency, fp8 gives better throughput at scale.
[02:36] Priya: can you show numbers?
[02:38] Marco: sure — here's a benchmark we ran on a 7B family model with 512 token context, p95 latency: baseline int8 = 105 ms, aggressive int8 = 92 ms, fp8 hybrid = 120 ms. Quality (task accuracy) baseline int8 = 98.6%, aggressive int8 = 97.9%, fp8 hybrid = 99.0%. cost delta: aggressive int8 ~ -18% cost vs baseline, fp8 ~ -12%.
[03:10] Priya: interesting, aggressive int8 improved latency and cost but slightly worse accuracy. sounds like a tradeoff we might accept.
[03:18] Sofia: exactly — that's where Redwood Optimize comes in: we recommend a quant profile per model and per route based on your evals. You can also do fallbacks or A/B routing: traffic goes to aggressive int8, with a small percentage to fp8 for monitoring.
[03:33] Liam: how do you do rollback on quality regressions?
[03:36] Marco: we integrate with our rollout system — canary at 5-10% traffic, automatic quality checks against your eval set; if thresholds fail we automatically rollback to the pinned version. All of that is visible in the Console.
[03:49] Nora: about KV cache — we saw mention in the doc, how does it affect tail latency?
[03:54] Marco: KV cache is key. cold starts that populate the cache can spike latency; for chat workloads with long contexts the first request after a cache miss might be slower. We do prefix caching and pre-warm strategies; Dedicated capacity with reserved GPU pools reduces cache churn and gives more stable p95.
[04:12] Priya: got it. and how much of a difference does Dedicated make vs Hosted?
[04:16] Marco: depends on traffic pattern. For steady traffic Dedicated can reduce p95 variance by 20-40% and is more cost predictable. Hosted is still good for spiky or small-scale; you get rapid onboarding.
[04:29] Priya: security questions — we need SOC2, SSO, KMS integration and audit logs. can you confirm?
[04:35] Sofia: yes, we have SOC2, SAML/SSO with SCIM provisioning, KMS integrations and audit logs. we'll share the security pack after this call.
[04:45] Liam: perfect. can you run benchmarks on our exact model? we have a proprietary 8B NLU model trained with domain tokens.
[04:53] Marco: absolutely, that's what the pilot is for. if you share a sample dataset and a docker or inference recipe we can run the same tests and return p95, p99, quality deltas, and cost estimates.
[05:05] Priya: timeline — we want a pilot next week, ideally start Feb 24 and run for 7 days.
[05:11] Sofia: sounds reasonable. we'll aim to deliver the benchmark spreadsheet within 48 hours of you sharing data.
[05:18] Marco: quick demo — switching to console — you'll see Optimize tab which lists models, recommended quant profile, expected latency and estimated token cost. I'm going to run a live micro-benchmark for the 7B example to show latency distributions.
[05:34] [screen share noises; some cross talk, transcription glitches]
[05:45] Marco: ok p95 plot is here — note tail spikes around cache misses. here's a table: baseline int8 p95 105ms, aggressive int8 p95 92ms, fp8 hybrid p95 120ms — same ballpark as the slide. also showing cost per 1k tokens.
[06:05] Priya: do you expose per-token cost by route? we need breakdown per feature.
[06:09] Marco: yes, Console gives per-route and per-model token cost and you can break down by API key. That helps with P&L of features.
[06:18] Nora: what about model fallbacks during capacity constraints? we have strict uptime SLOs.
[06:22] Marco: Smart routing can fallback to a compatible model variant — for example if 8B INT8 is not available we can route to a 6B variant or to fp8 mode in a different region. There are policies you set: prioritize latency, prioritize cost, or prefer same-region.
[06:37] Priya: ok curious about quantization artifacts — hallucination increase or embedding drift?
[06:42] Marco: aggressive int8 can slightly increase hallucination in NLG cases; for classification/embedding tasks it's mostly embedding drift. We measure embedding cosine delta and precision/recall on your labeled set. For sensitive entities we recommend fp8 hybrid or keeping key layers in fp16.
[06:55] Sofia: just to chime in — many customers choose mixed profiles per route: e.g., short chat replies use aggressive int8 for latency, while long-form generation or safety-sensitive routes use fp8 or fp16.
[07:08] Liam: ok can you talk about hardware implications — which GPUs is this optimized for?
[07:13] Marco: we optimize across NVIDIA and AMD on-prem stacks; for int8 we leverage tensor cores where available. fp8 kernels are newer and performance depends on driver/runtime; our runtime will pick the best kernel automatically. If you're deploying Private on your own infra we ship optimizations and kernel picks with the runtime.
[07:31] Priya: we have A100s in prod, but on the edge we have T4s for throughput. will that matter?
[07:36] Marco: T4s have different performance profiles; int8 often gets great gains on A100 with tensor cores, T4 may be less dramatic. We'll include per-hardware numbers in the pilot.
[07:47] Nora: how intrusive is integration? we have a CI/CD pipeline we don't want to change much.
[07:51] Sofia: integration is via API or private control plane. for Dedicated you get a stable endpoint and a small agent/runtime if you go Private on prem. Most customers integrate with minimal code changes.
[08:03] [10 minute mark — conversation continues with deeper Qs on evals and pilot setup]
[08:05] Marco: for the benchmark we ask for: 1) sample inference dataset (1k rows preferred), 2) labeled eval set if available, 3) target SLOs and expected qps. we'll run 512-token and 128-token scenarios to measure sensitivity to sequence length.
[08:20] Priya: we can provide that. Our model often uses 256 token average but spikes to 1024 on long conversations.
[08:28] Marco: that's important — sequence length changes the memory and kernel selection behavior; int8 advantage increases with longer sequences for memory-bound workloads.
[08:39] Priya: about cost math — you quoted per-token before, how do we map that to our pricing?
[08:44] Sofia: we'll send a cost calc sheet — cost per 1k tokens by profile and by model. The Console's cost estimator also shows projected monthly cost given QPS and average tokens.
[08:56] Liam: question on compliance — do you support customer-managed keys for Private?
[09:00] Marco: yes, KMS/HSM and customer-managed keys are supported for Private; for Dedicated we can integrate with your cloud KMS. Audit logs are exportable to your SIEM.
[09:10] Priya: great. one sticking point — latency at p99; we saw 300ms p99 in some public benchmarks. we need p99 < 250ms ideally.
[09:18] Marco: p99 is influenced by cache and bursting; Dedicated with reserved GPU pools and pre-warmed instances is the best path to tighten p99. Also tuning batching windows — small micro batching can reduce cost but increase p99; Optimize recommends per-route batching settings.
[09:36] Sofia: want to show an example routing policy? if latency-critical route we set max_batch_size=1 and disable micro-batching, pin to low-latency nodes. For high-throughput we enable batching and a quant profile that maximizes throughput.
[09:51] Priya: could Redwood run the pilot on our infra or do we need to push models to Redwood?
[09:57] Marco: flexible — we can run on Redwood Hosted using your data (with contracts), or run with a Private deployment in your VPC. For an initial 7-day pilot, many customers choose Hosted with strict data handling and an NDA in place.
[10:12] Liam: for Hosted do you retain data? Our security team will want retention controls.
[10:16] Sofia: retention controls are configurable; we can set short retention windows or no retention for inference payloads in pilot. We'll include that in the security doc.
[10:25] [Mid-call technical deep dive — Marco shows console drilldowns and logs]
[10:30] Marco: here's the evaluation view: we run your eval set across profiles and compute delta metrics, and the Console flags regressions > threshold. You can also instrument custom metrics and push back to Redwood for monitoring.
[10:45] Priya: any gotchas with tokenization differences when we run bench on our model vs Redwood reference?
[10:51] Marco: tokenization must match — we ask for the same tokenizer and preproc, or we containerize your inference to avoid mismatch. small tokenization diffs can skew per-token cost and quality numbers.
[11:02] Nora: what about model quantization toolchain — do you do post-training quant or do you need quant-aware training?
[11:08] Marco: we support post-training quant with calibration; quant-aware training is ideal for aggressive int8 but not always necessary. For some models we recommend a short calibration pass to collect activation ranges.
[11:18] Priya: ok that fits our timeline.
[11:21] Marco: last section — demoing rollout UI: you can schedule canary, set quality thresholds, and tie alerts to Slack/PagerDuty. If a threshold trips, the system will revert automatically.
[11:33] Sofia: recap and next steps — Priya to share dataset and SLOs by 2026-02-22, Marco to run benchmarks and share spreadsheet by 2026-02-25, Sofia to send pricing, security pack and pilot contract. plan pilot start 2026-02-24.
[11:50] Priya: thanks all, this was helpful. any outstanding risks? I'd flag hardware differences (A100 vs T4) and tokenization mismatches as primary.
[12:00] Marco: agreed, we'll include per-hardware profiles and a tokenizer checklist.
[12:06] Nora: ok will expect the docs.
[12:10] Sofia: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the attachments and the meeting notes.
[12:16] Priya: thanks.
[12:20] [call ends]
